Aging SCF wealth between survey waves

Twelve three-year projections, 1989 to 2025, scored against the next survey

Published

October 10, 2026

Models that need current household wealth take the latest Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) and grow it with aggregates from the Federal Reserve’s Financial Accounts. This report projects every SCF wave from 1989 to 2022 three years forward with four methods and scores each projection against the wave that followed. The last pair, 2022→2025, ends in the survey the Fed published on 9 October 2026.

The design was written down and tagged (prereg-v1) before the 2025 microdata were opened: methods, statistics, scores and the rules for calling a winner. The eleven pairs through 2019→2022 were in view while the methods were built, and one method was changed after looking at them, as the specification records. The Fed’s report had already given the 2025 mean and median, so a blind level score, over the 25th, 75th, 90th and 99th percentiles, carries the cleanest test.

Summary

  • The 2022→2025 test. The lowest level score, over the mean and five percentiles, belongs to (d) DFA groups (5.6%, against 8.8% for no change). The lowest blind level score, which leaves out the already-published mean and median, belongs to (c) Asset class (5.9% against 11.1%). The ranking from the development pairs held: (c) beat both (a) and (b) on the level and blind level scores.
  • Every aging method overshot the 2025 mean, by +7.3% to +8.6%, outside sampling noise; holding dollars fixed missed it by -5.9%, within noise. Financial Accounts household net worth grew 14.1% in real terms per household; the SCF mean grew 6.3%. For asset-class scaling the overshoot is equities: its projected mean was $106k per family too high, equities contributed $106k, and the other six classes together -$0.7k. The Financial Accounts equity series grew 54% in real terms per household; mean SCF equity holdings grew 20%.
  • No method caught the fall in the top 1% share, from 35.1% to 31.3%. All four overshot it by 3.2 to 6.1 points, outside noise; DFA scaling, which grew the top groups fastest, missed by the most.
  • On subgroup medians doing nothing did best in 2025. Every method, including no change, overshot the under-35 median by +31% to +49%. A projection moves dollars, not people, so it cannot follow a change in who holds what within an age group.
  • Over all twelve pairs, asset-class scaling has the lowest mean level score of the three methods that use no SCF information from the target (10.7%, against 11.5% for uniform scaling and 13.8% for no change). Pair by pair it is less dependable: uniform scaling beats no change on 7 of 12 pairs and asset-class scaling on 7.
  • The ceiling is low. Scaling each class by the SCF’s own growth, which no forecaster has, still leaves a mean level error of 7.1% across the twelve pairs. That remainder is change in the shape of the distribution that scaling by aggregates, even the right ones, does not capture.

The public file differs from the internal one the report is built from. Per the SCF codebooks it leaves out respondents wealthy enough for the Forbes list (7 of 4,602 in 2022 and 7 of 4,367 in 2025) and rounds and blurs dollar values. Dropping the wealthiest respondents lowers the mean more than the median, which fits the gaps above.

Method

The full specification is in PREREGISTRATION.md; the source for each claim about the underlying data is in docs/sources.md.

  • Data. SCF Summary Extract Public Data, thirteen waves, all in 2025 dollars as reissued by the Fed on 9 October 2026. Family-level, weighted, five implicates.
  • Factor. Nominal growth of a Financial Accounts aggregate between the third quarters of the two survey years, divided by growth in the number of households (Census, CPS ASEC) and by growth in the September CPI-U-RS the Fed uses to deflate the SCF.
  • (a) No change. Real amounts held fixed.
  • (b) Uniform. One factor from household net worth (BOGZ1FL192090005Q).
  • (c) Asset class. Seven classes that sum to net worth, each with the factor for its Financial Accounts series.
  • (d) DFA groups. Households placed in the DFA’s five wealth groups; assets scaled by the group’s DFA assets, debt by its DFA liabilities.
  • Scoring. Statistics computed on each implicate and averaged. Standard errors from the 999 replicate weights plus 6/5 of the between-implicate variance, as the SCF codebook prescribes.
  • Unchanged by construction. Weights, households and demographics. A projection moves dollars only: nobody ages, forms a household, buys a first home or retires.

Limits. The SCF and Financial Accounts classes do not match exactly; the specification lists each mismatch. The Financial Accounts levels are today’s vintage, so historical pairs use revised data. Whether any Financial Accounts household series is itself benchmarked to the SCF was not checked; if one is, (b) and (c) are partly in-sample on the historical pairs. Within-noise is a failure to reject, not evidence of accuracy.

Reproduce

uv sync
uv run pytest
uv run python -m wealthdata.backtest
./scripts/render_report.sh
